newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russian unions predict big turnout on strike day.
newsitem.headline: Russian unions predict big turnout on strike day.

text.p: Russian trade union leaders said on Tuesday they expected more than 20 million people to join a nationwide day of protest on Thursday and promised special security measures to stop things getting out of hand.

But previous rallies complaining about wage arrears and government policy have attracted far lower crowds than forecast and it was not clear whether the long-apathetic Russians would take to the streets in numbers this time.
The protesters, backed by Russia's communist opposition, are complaining about massive backlogs in paying wages and pensions.
Unions say workers and pensioners are owed 50 trillion roubles ($8.8 billion) including 10 trillion owed by the state.

"About 20 million people will take part in the actions. Warning strikes will be held at 29,000 enterprises, more than 300 towns and villages will hold meetings and demonstrations or will picket administration buildings," the Federation of Independent Trade Unions said in a statement.
Federation Chairman Mikhail Shmakov said special security measures would be in place to ensure the protests were peaceful, but he did not expect trouble.
"The trade unions are making every effort to ensure all protest actions are carried out in accordance with the law...and in full cooperation with law-enforcement organs," he told a news conference.
The Russian press has warned that rogue elements among the strikers were planning "provocative acts" and Russian television on Monday showed police training in crowd control techniques.
The state, for its part, was scrambling to pay angry workers before Thursday, but government spokesman Igor Shabdurasulov said on Tuesday that this could not happen overnight.

"I wouldn't expect any revolutionary decisions in the next three-five days, fortnight, or even month on issues such as natural monopolies, social issues or other problems," Shabdurasulov told a news conference.
"It's not real to imagine solving such a series of problems tomorrow or the day after tomorrow."
He said a timetable was being organised to set out realistic goals. Back pensions would be paid by the end of June, debts to teachers by May, and government debts by the autumn.
Shmakov said he expected full payment sooner.
"A schedule of payments is being worked up for each sector of the economy and for each trade union," he said.
"We are sure the problem of liquidating the arrears in wages can be resolved in the course of three to four months... The government holds all the cards to be able to deal with the problem."
In Moscow, workers plan to picket the White House government building and to march through the centre of the capital.
Shmakov said about 100,000 people would take part.
